Content:
Suppose the Taylor (Maclaurin) series for the function [MATH: f(x)] about [MATH: x=0] is given by
[MATH: f(x) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \dfrac{(-1)^n}{2n+1} x^{2n+1}]

Content:
All we need to do is differentiate the Taylor series of [MATH: f(x).] Writing out the first three terms, we get
[MATH: f(x) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \dfrac{(-1)^n}{2n+1} x^{2n+1} = x - \dfrac{x^3}{3} + \dfrac{x^5}{5} - \cdots.]

Content:
Now, to find [MATH: f'(x),] we differentiate term-by-term and get
[MATH: f^{′}(x)|= (d)/(dx)(x) − (d)/(dx)((x^{3})/(3)) + (d)/(dx)((x^{5})/(5)) − ⋯; = 1 − x^{2} + x^{4} − ⋯.]

And that's it! The radius of convergence of the Taylor series for [MATH: f'(x)] is [MATH: R,] the same as [MATH: f(x).]

sections.normalized_html: The Taylor series for the function [MATH: f(x)] about [MATH: x=0] is given by [MATH: \displaystyle f(x) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{(-3)^{n}\,x^n}{n^3}] The series converges to [MATH: f(x)] for [MATH: |x| < R,] where [MATH: R] is the radius of convergence of the Taylor series. Calculate the radius of convergence of the series expansion of [MATH: f'(x),] the derivative of [MATH: f(x),] about [MATH: x=0.]

The Taylor series for the function [MATH: f(x)] about [MATH: x=0] is given by
[MATH: \displaystyle f(x) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{(-3)^{n}\,x^n}{n^3}]
The series converges to [MATH: f(x)] for [MATH: |x| < R,] where [MATH: R] is the radius of convergence of the Taylor series. Calculate the radius of convergence of the series expansion of [MATH: f'(x),] the derivative of [MATH: f(x),] about [MATH: x=0.]

sections.normalized_html:
The radius of convergence for the Taylor series of [MATH: f'(x)] is the same as the Taylor series of [MATH: f(x).] So, to find the radius of convergence of [MATH: f'(x),] we need to compute [MATH: R.]

To calculate [MATH: R,] we can use the ratio test. Computing the limit of the absolute value of the ratio of two consecutive terms, we get [MATH: L|= lim_(n → ∞)|(a_{n + 1})/(a_{n})|; = lim_(n → ∞)|((− 3)^{n + 1}x^{n + 1})/((n + 1)^{3}) ⋅ (n^{3})/((− 3)^{n}x^{n})|; = lim_(n → ∞)|((− 3)x ⋅ n^{3})/((n + 1)^{3})|; = 3|x|lim_(n → ∞)(1)/((1 + (1)/(n))^{3}); = 3|x|.]

The series converges when [MATH: L<1.] So, it converges when

[MATH: 3|x||< 1;|x||< (1)/(3)]

Therefore, the radius of convergence is [MATH: R = \dfrac 1 3.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

And that's it! The radius of convergence of the Taylor series for [MATH: f'(x)] is [MATH: R,] the same as [MATH: f(x).]
